defaults.permitted_development: Across Kent, the ordinary householder route for a fence, wall or gate usually depends on the height and its relationship to the road: 1 metre by a vehicular highway, 2 metres elsewhere. Listed-building settings and removed rights can change that answer quickly. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Kent, for ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Across Kent, means of enclosure are not controlled by an extension-style depth formula. Height, siting and visual effect do the main planning work.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Kent, the same boundary treatment can be acceptable in one position and need permission in another once it fronts a road or sits on a prominent corner.
rules.roof_rules: Across Kent, canopies or roofed gate features need their own planning check.
rules.materials_rules: Across Kent, there is no prescribed material palette for ordinary fences and walls, but prominent frontages are easiest to justify when the boundary treatment fits the surrounding street character.

restrictions.conservation_area: Boundary works in conservation areas are more sensitive because removal as well as replacement can affect the character and appearance of the area.
restrictions.listed_building: If the property is listed, or the boundary adjoins listed curtilage structures, changing the enclosure can need listed building consent as well as planning review.
restrictions.article4_notes: A planning condition or Article 4 direction can override the standard boundary limits, so even a straightforward replacement fence may need consent.

rules.permitted_development: In most straightforward house cases, a new or altered boundary treatment can rely on permitted development up to 1 metre by the highway and 2 metres in other positions. The important exceptions are heritage curtilages, Article 4 areas and schemes that increase an already excessive height. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: For ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Boundary can still need permission because of its position and visual impact even though there is no formal depth limit.
rules.boundary_rules: Front and corner boundaries often need more careful design than enclosed rear-garden boundaries.
rules.roof_rules: A simple gate or wall is one thing; a roofed gate feature can be quite another. Covered entrance elements should not be assumed to sit within the same fallback.
rules.materials_rules: National planning rules focus on height and siting rather than a fixed material list, but visible front boundaries should still use finishes that suit the house and street. Heritage areas are more demanding on detail.

restrictions.conservation_area: Boundary works in conservation areas are more sensitive because removal as well as replacement can affect the character and appearance of the area.
restrictions.listed_building: Boundary works to or around a listed building can require listed building consent, especially where historic walls, railings, piers or gates are being altered or removed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Normal enclosure rights can be withdrawn by Article 4 directions or by conditions on the property, which is why front-boundary work sometimes still needs an application.
